slides.title: Chapter 3: Bitcoin Core
slides.say: Chapter 2 followed one payment through the network. Chapter 3 opens the program that checks every rule, Bitcoin Core, and shows how to build it, run it and ask it questions. Every result in this deck was computed by the chapter library from saved data.

slides.title: Today's route
slides.say: The route has seven parts that follow the program from its source code to the toolkits around it. Three true stories and nineteen code examples are spread across them. Every example has a picture of its result.
slides.takeaway: Seven parts, three true stories, nineteen examples

slides.title: The questions this chapter answers
slides.say: The six questions are the chapter's own, rewritten so that each has an answer on a slide. We return to them in the summary. A reader who can answer all six has understood the chapter.

slides.title: The chapter in one picture
slides.say: Six steps carry us from the source code to the data of the chain. We read the code and pick a release, build it, run it, ask it questions and read what it says. The last step looks at other programs that speak to a node.
slides.takeaway: Six steps from the source code to the data of the chain

slides.title: From Bitcoin to Bitcoin Core
slides.say: Part 1 asks what Bitcoin Core is. It began as the program Satoshi Nakamoto released in 2009, and it checks every rule itself as a full verification node. Changes reach it through numbered Bitcoin Improvement Proposals.
slides.takeaway: Bitcoin Core: The Reference Implementation

slides.title: Version 0.1, set in stone
slides.say: In January 2009 Satoshi Nakamoto published version 0.1 of the Bitcoin program. A year and a half later he wrote that its core design was set in stone. That is why Bitcoin Core is called the reference implementation: the software came first, and the rules are what it does.
slides.takeaway: The program came first: the reference implementation defines the rules

slides.title: Inside the program
slides.say: Bitcoin Core is one program with several parts. Peers and the connection manager bring in blocks and transactions, the validation engine checks them, and the storage engine keeps headers, blocks and coins. The interface at the right lets your own programs ask questions.
slides.takeaway: One program: it listens, checks, stores and answers

slides.title: A version number that carries a vote
slides.say: A block's version field is not a counter. Its top three bits mark the BIP 9 scheme, and every lower bit is a vote for one proposal. Here only bit 1 is set.
slides.takeaway: Think of a ballot with 29 tick boxes, one for each proposal

slides.title: Bitcoin Development Environment
slides.say: Part 2 turns the source code into programs you can run. A release tag fixes which version you build, and release candidates are tried before a final tag exists. The build produces bitcoind, the node itself.
slides.takeaway: Compiling Bitcoin Core from the Source Code

slides.title: Three steps from source to executables
slides.say: A build has three decisions. You select a release tag, you configure which features to build, and you build the executables. Each step has a single command, and a clean tag makes the result repeatable.
slides.takeaway: Select, configure, build: three steps, one set of programs

slides.title: Release tags sort by number, not by letters
slides.say: These are real tags of the Bitcoin repository. Sorted as text, v0.10.0 lands before v0.9.5, which is wrong. A release candidate is a tag with rc in it, so we leave those out first.
slides.takeaway: Think of edition numbers: the tenth edition follows the ninth

slides.title: What a release folder holds
slides.say: A release unpacks into seven programs and three helper parts. The one to know is bitcoind, the node. You steer it from the command line with bitcoin-cli.
slides.takeaway: Think of bitcoind as the engine and bitcoin-cli as the steering wheel

slides.title: Dozens of builders, one identical binary
slides.say: Anyone can ask whether a downloaded binary really matches the source. Since release 22.0 Bitcoin Core builds with Guix, so independent builders get identical files and sign their hashes. For release 31.1 the checksum file carries eleven good signatures.
slides.takeaway: Verify, don't trust: the project applies its own rule to itself

slides.title: A download must match its published hash
slides.say: Each release ships a list of hashes. You hash your download and compare. If the two texts match, the file is the one that the builders signed for.
slides.takeaway: Think of the safety seal on a medicine bottle: break it and you can tell

slides.title: Running a Bitcoin Core Node
slides.say: Part 3 starts the node and sets it up. A configuration file and the command line decide what the node does, and the data directory is where it keeps everything. Pruning, the transaction index and the memory limits trade disk, memory and features.
slides.takeaway: Configuring the Bitcoin Core Node

slides.title: The command line wins over the file
slides.say: A configuration file holds the settings of a node. When the same option is also given on the command line, the command line wins. A script can therefore change one value for one run.
slides.takeaway: Think of a recipe card that you may override with a note on the fridge

slides.title: Inside the data directory
slides.say: Everything the node knows lives in its data directory. Blocks and the chain state are the big parts, the log is the node's diary, and the configuration file holds your settings. The cookie file appears while the node runs.
slides.takeaway: The data directory is the whole memory of the node

slides.title: How the database cache is shared out
slides.say: The dbcache option sizes the cache for the unspent outputs. Bitcoin Core first gives two small databases their share. Everything else goes to the cache of coins.
slides.takeaway: Think of a desk: two small drawers and one very large tabletop

slides.title: Pruning and the transaction index do not mix
slides.say: Pruning keeps only recent blocks. The transaction index must find any block that holds a transaction. The node therefore refuses both at once, and release 31.1 printed exactly that.
slides.takeaway: Think of a library that shreds old books and so cannot catalogue them all

slides.title: Two ways to spend less memory
slides.say: Two settings reduce what a node asks of its machine. Blocks-only mode stops it from collecting loose transactions, and the mempool limit caps the waiting room. The default limit is 300 megabytes, and blocks-only mode needs only 5.
slides.takeaway: A node can trade features for memory, and keep verifying everything

slides.title: An alert text is cleaned before it runs
slides.say: The node can run a script of yours when something is wrong. The message goes into the command, so the node cleans it first. The hostile quotes vanish and the rest stays inside one word.
slides.takeaway: Think of a mail room that removes anything dangerous before a letter reaches you

slides.title: The project that outlives its keyholders
slides.say: Bitcoin Core outlived its first author. Satoshi Nakamoto handed the project to Gavin Andresen in 2011, and on 7 April 2014 Andresen passed the lead to Wladimir van der Laan. A reference implementation needs a team and public review, not one keyholder.
slides.takeaway: The reference implementation is an institution, not a person

slides.title: Bitcoin Core API
slides.say: Part 4 talks to the running node. The command-line client bitcoin-cli sends JSON-RPC calls, and the node checks who is asking before it answers. The cookie is the default way in, and rpcauth is the fixed alternative.
slides.takeaway: Getting Information on Bitcoin Core's Status

slides.title: One JSON-RPC call and its reply
slides.say: A call is a small JSON text with a method and parameters. The reply carries a result, an error and the id of the call. The sample reply is the one the book prints for the curl example.
slides.takeaway: Think of an order slip: the same fields every time, and an answer on the same slip

slides.title: The cookie is a fresh password
slides.say: At every start bitcoind writes a new random secret to the .cookie file. A client that can read the file can call the node. The secret is 32 bytes, shown as 64 hexadecimal characters.
slides.takeaway: Think of a hotel key card that is recoded for every guest

slides.title: rpcauth stores a salted hash, not the password
slides.say: The rpcauth line holds a user, a random salt and a keyed hash of the password. Even a leaked configuration file does not reveal the password. A wrong password gives a different hash.
slides.takeaway: Think of a bank that keeps a check value and never your PIN

slides.title: Reading getblockchaininfo
slides.say: This is the answer of a real node of release 31.1 that had only the first block. It says which chain it is on, how many blocks it has verified and how hard the work is.
slides.takeaway: Think of a car dashboard: it reports, and you do not touch the engine

slides.title: Exploring and Decoding Transactions
slides.say: Part 5 reads a transaction the way the node reports it. Each transaction has an identifier, a weight and a witness. We decode Alice's payment from chapter 2 and look at each part.
slides.takeaway: Reading a transaction the way the node reports it

slides.title: Decoding Alice's transaction
slides.say: The node's own decoder turns Alice's bytes into readable fields. Every output has a number, a value and a type. Two outputs, 20,000 and 75,000 satoshis, plus the 5,000 fee make her 100,000.
slides.takeaway: Think of an X-ray: the same body, shown layer by layer

slides.title: The txid leaves the witness out
slides.say: The txid is a hash of the transaction without its witness. A third party can no longer change the txid by re-encoding a signature. That change is called transaction malleability, and segregated witness ended it.
slides.takeaway: Think of a tracking number printed before anyone adds a signature

slides.title: Weight units and virtual bytes
slides.say: Blocks are filled by weight units. Base bytes count four units each and witness bytes one. Alice's 194 bytes weigh 569 units, which is 143 virtual bytes.
slides.takeaway: Think of postage by volume: compact, light data costs less

slides.title: Exploring Blocks
slides.say: Part 6 reads blocks. A block has a height, a hash made from its header, a merkle root of its transactions and a time. We rebuild each one ourselves with a few lines of Python.
slides.takeaway: Height, hash, merkle root and time

slides.title: Height, depth and confirmations
slides.say: A block's height counts the blocks before it, so the first block has height zero. Each block built on top adds a confirmation. The numbers in the picture are an example, not a live chain.
slides.takeaway: A confirmation is one more block on top of yours

slides.title: A block's name is the hash of its header
slides.say: The header has six fields in 80 bytes. Hashing it twice and reversing the bytes gives the block hash, which starts with many zeros. The block's height, 123,456, counts the blocks before it.
slides.takeaway: Think of a fingerprint taken from the page's header line

slides.title: Rebuilding the merkle root
slides.say: Block 123,456 holds 13 transactions. Hashing neighbours in pairs gives 7, 4, 2 and finally 1 hash. That last hash is the merkle root stored in the header, and one changed transaction would change it.
slides.takeaway: Think of a tournament bracket: pairs play, winners meet, one champion remains

slides.title: Median time of the last eleven blocks
slides.say: Miners write the time into every header, and it can be a little off. Bitcoin Core therefore uses the median of the last eleven times. We recompute the saved median of block 123,456.
slides.takeaway: Think of a median price that one odd sale cannot move

slides.title: Alternative Clients, Libraries, and Toolkits
slides.say: Part 7 looks beyond Bitcoin Core. Libraries such as python-bitcoinlib call the node from your own programs, and other clients follow the same rules in other languages. We end with how fresh each toolkit is.
slides.takeaway: Using Bitcoin Core's Programmatic Interface

slides.title: Using Bitcoin Core's Programmatic Interface
slides.say: A library can speak to the node for you. python-bitcoinlib builds the JSON-RPC call, sends it over HTTP and returns the result as a Python value. On the offline node of release 31.1 a call for the block count returned zero.
slides.takeaway: Your code can ask the node anything the command line can

slides.title: How fresh are the alternative toolkits
slides.say: Libraries for other languages and other clients exist, but they age. This is the number of days between each toolkit's latest release and the day we asked the registries. A library can be useful and still be old.
slides.takeaway: Think of the date on the newest delivery in a shop window

slides.title: Summary: the six answers
slides.say: Each row answers one of the six opening questions in a line. If you can say each answer in your own words, using the everyday pictures of this chapter, you have the chapter.
slides.takeaway: Reference, release, settings, interface, transaction, block

slides.say: These links are all open and free. Start with the chapter source and the release page, try the RPC reference against your own node, and watch the talk on tracing a running node. The community links are where questions get answered.
